analysis.one_liner: Orders a federal study of land around Walnut Canyon National Monument to weigh conservation and recreation options.
analysis.headline: The bill to study 30,818 acres around Walnut Canyon National Monument was referred to committee on March 16, 2007, and never received a vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Interior and Agriculture departments to jointly study about 30,800 acres around Walnut Canyon National Monument in Arizona, including national forest, state, private, and monument land. The study would evaluate the area's resources, existing public uses like hunting, grazing, and camping, and management options ranging from a monument boundary adjustment to a National Recreation Area designation to leaving it with the Forest Service. It authorized $350,000 for the work and required a report to Congress within 18 months of funding.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or visit Walnut Canyon east of Flagstaff, Arizona. The study would have weighed whether roughly 30,800 acres around the monument — used today for hiking, hunting, grazing, camping, and other recreation — should be better protected from pressures like urban development while keeping those public uses intact. Local governments in Flagstaff and Coconino County would also have had a formal seat in shaping the study.

how_it_helps.text: It would fund a formal study of the resources, public uses, and management options for the land around Walnut Canyon National Monument, giving Congress a basis for future decisions instead of ad hoc ones.

The study was required to weigh ways to protect archaeological sites, watershed health, and scenery while maintaining existing public uses — from hiking and hunting to grazing and firewood gathering — so recreation access would stay on the table.
It required collaboration with the Flagstaff City Council and the Coconino County Board of Supervisors, giving local communities a formal role in the process.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund it: the bill authorizes up to $350,000 for the study, plus staff time at the Forest Service and National Park Service. No landowner would have to give up anything under the bill itself, since it explicitly leaves current management unchanged.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorized $350,000 in taxpayer money for a study that would not change anything on its own — the bill states that nothing in it affects current management of the land.

A recommendation for a monument boundary adjustment or National Recreation Area designation could later restrict uses like grazing, hunting, or development on the 2,037 acres of state land and 214 acres of private land inside the study area.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost was small — $350,000 for a study — and the potential benefit modest but real: a thoughtful look at how to protect archaeological sites, scenery, and watershed health on land just outside a growing city, while explicitly preserving hunting, grazing, and other existing public uses. The honest weakness is that a study binds no one; it would only have set up a later, separate fight over any actual designation, and property and state-land interests inside the study area had reason to watch that closely.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then a subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for action before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Rick Renzi introduced the bill on March 16, 2007, and it was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee.
On March 19, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands.
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind followed, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost anything of consequence. Land management around Walnut Canyon continued as before; the main effect of the bill's death is that no study recommendations were produced for Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the status quo continued

for.name: Rick Renzi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote on the bill after receiving the referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill had minimal, slightly bipartisan sponsorship — one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and died in committee without any recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation users and outfitters around Walnut Canyon
industries.note: The bill would not have changed any management itself, but a study favoring stronger protection could have shaped future decisions on land used for hunting, grazing, camping, snowmobiling, and other recreation near Flagstaff. The bill specifically required the study to consider keeping existing public uses intact.

The study area includes 2,037 acres of state land and 214 acres of private land, and one option to be studied was a monument boundary adjustment that could bring more land under federal management. The bill itself changed nothing, but its purpose was to build a record for possible future designation.
